Claude Code's plan mode is linear and inflexible: it writes a giant plan and rewrites the whole thing after feedback. "IMO Superpowers isn't the ideal solution because it too lacks flexibility, but including the 'plan sketch' stage is sure an improvement."

Overall useful. Core workflow: brainstorm a spec, subagents review it, write a plan, subagents implement with TDD. The brainstorming skill is great for fleshing out rough ideas, and adversarial subagent review of the spec/plan "has caught several things I would've missed." Dislikes the spec/plan split; the plan often ends up as code blocks in a Markdown doc.
Agrees the implementation plan isn't that useful to read; often just tells it to go after reading the design doc.
A recent update removed the subagents for self-review; the self-review now happens in the main agent.
The install mechanism for Codex and OpenCode is "interesting": you tell the agent to fetch and follow instructions from a raw GitHub INSTALL.md. "it's like curl|bash but with added LLM agents..."

"I personally don't like superpowers very much. My boss does. I think Claude makes more mistakes when using superpowers than when not." Still recommends trying it, but it's no silver bullet: "It's still the same Claude." Their own prompting style is already similar to what it does under the hood.

As a solo programmer, always converges on staying heavily involved in planning and code review, working in steps of finer granularity than Superpowers suggests. This produces less code, but it's the only way they know to discover less code is needed.
